title: Do we still need the office?
summary_es: Tres directivos discuten qué hacer con la oficina cuando venza el alquiler: renovar, reducir o dejarla. Acaban pactando un término medio.
prediction_prompt: What do people gain, and what do they lose, when a company gives up its office?

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Right, shall we make a start? The lease on this building runs out in March.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: So the question on the table is simple: do we renew it, shrink it, or give it up?

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: From a purely financial point of view, it's hard to justify renewing.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: On an average day, barely a third of the desks are occupied.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: We're effectively paying rent on a very expensive storage room.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: I'd push back on that a little, Marcus. Occupancy isn't the only measure of value.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: Go on.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: When we surveyed staff in the autumn, the picture was more mixed than you'd think.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: Most people love the flexibility. But nearly half said they feel less connected to their teams.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: And among people who joined in the last two years, that figure rises to seventy per cent.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: That's the part that bothers me. The newcomers.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: You can't learn how a company really works from a screen.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: With respect, that sounds like nostalgia. Plenty of firms have no office at all.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: They do, and some of them are struggling to keep their junior staff.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: New people learn by overhearing: how a colleague handles a difficult client, say.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: None of that happens on a scheduled video call.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: And what do our clients make of it? Do they still expect to visit us?

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: Fewer than before, but the big ones do like to see where their money goes.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: Fine, but we can't keep three floors for the sake of overheard conversations.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Nobody's suggesting three floors. What would one floor save us?

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: Roughly sixty per cent of what we spend now. Giving up the building altogether saves everything, obviously.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: And costs us in other ways. We'd be hiring meeting rooms every week.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Let me try a middle path. We keep one floor and redesign it completely.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Fewer desks, more rooms where teams can actually work together.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: And we ask each team to choose two days when everyone is in the office.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: Choose, or be told? Because if it's optional, we'll be back here in a year.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: Teams choose the days, but turning up on those days isn't optional. That's the deal.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: I could live with that, provided we review the numbers after six months.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Agreed. If the floor is still half empty by September, we think again.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: And the savings? I'd rather they didn't simply disappear into the general budget.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: Could part of it go towards bringing remote staff in a few times a year?

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: Some of them haven't met their own managers in person.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: I like that. Marcus, can you cost it?

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: I'll have figures by Friday. Don't expect miracles.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: I never do.

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: One more thing. Whatever we decide, we should explain the reasoning, not just the result.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Absolutely. People will accept a compromise if they can see how we arrived at it.

segments.speaker: marcus
segments.text: That I can agree with.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: So, to summarise: one floor, two fixed team days, a six-month review.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: And a proposal on travel for remote staff. Anything else?

segments.speaker: jo
segments.text: Only that we tell people before the rumours do it for us.

segments.speaker: claire
segments.text: Good point. I'll draft something tonight. Thanks, both.

connected_speech.explanation_es: *shall* se reduce a /ʃəl/ y *make a* se enlaza.

connected_speech.phrase: barely a third of the desks are occupied
connected_speech.ipa: /ˈbeəli ə ˈθɜːd əv ðə ˈdesks ər ˈɒkjupaɪd/
connected_speech.explanation_es: *of* y *are* son débiles (/əv/, /ər/), y *are occupied* se enlaza.
En británico *can't* tiene vocal larga /ɑː/; la *t* apenas suena.

connected_speech.phrase: for the sake of overheard conversations
I could live with that, provided we review
I'd rather they didn't simply disappear
connected_speech.explanation_es: *I'd rather* + pasado expresa una preferencia sobre lo que hagan otros. *didn't* pierde la *t*.

connected_speech.phrase: we'll be back here in a year
connected_speech.ipa: /wiːl bi ˈbæk hɪər ɪn ə ˈjɪə/
connected_speech.explanation_es: *we'll* casi no se oye y *here in a* se dice seguido.
